analysis.one_liner: Requires makers of cribs, toys, and small appliances to register buyers so they can be notified directly about recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to a House subcommittee in March 2005, it sat without a hearing or action until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a rule requiring manufacturers of children's products (cribs, strollers, high chairs, toys) and small appliances to set up a way to reach buyers directly when a product is recalled — through a simple registration card with no marketing questions, online registration, or tags and bar codes. It responded to the problem that recall news reaches very few buyers: manufacturers know how to contact only about 7% of the people who own their products. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children and households that own small appliances like toasters, blenders, and coffee makers. Today a recall is only as good as the news coverage or store posting behind it; under the bill, the manufacturer would have to keep a registration list and contact buyers directly, which the CPSC found is one of the most effective ways to get a recalled product out of a home. The bill's own findings note the CPSC runs roughly 300 recalls a year but can reach fewer than 7% of buyers directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and owners of children's products

how_it_helps.text: Direct contact is one of the most effective ways to get consumers to respond to a recall, according to CPSC research cited in the bill; today manufacturers have contact information for fewer than 7% of buyers, so most recalled cribs, strollers, and appliances stay in use.

The bill would have required a simplified 'product safety owner card' that asks only for the minimum information needed to reach the buyer in a recall — no marketing questions — plus options like online registration, electronic tags, and bar codes.

The approach had a working precedent: since 1993, the same simple registration cards have been required on child car seats, and the bill's findings state that this measurably increased recall compliance.

Coverage was targeted where the danger is greatest: any durable product intended for children under 5 — cribs, toddler beds, high chairs, bath seats, playpens, strollers, walkers, swings, bassinets, and toys — plus small kitchen appliances, with the Commission able to add other product categories.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of juvenile products and small household appliances, who would have to design, print, and process registration cards or run online registration systems and maintain recall databases. Those costs would partly show up in product prices, and companies that use registration data for marketing would lose the ability to harvest it — the bill limits the database to recall notification only. The CPSC would also take on new rulemaking work under tight deadlines: a proposed rule within 90 days and a final rule within 270 days of enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: makers of cribs, strollers, toys, and appliances

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on manufacturers, including smaller toy and appliance makers, and would likely be passed through to consumers in prices — a real cost for a safety benefit that only pays off when a recall actually happens.

The bill creates new consumer databases held by private companies. It restricts the data to recall notification only, but any system that collects buyer contact information raises privacy questions a skeptic would reasonably press.

Registration cards only work if consumers fill them out. The bill's own findings show 93% of buyers discard the current cards because they ask for marketing and personal information, and there is no guarantee that even a simplified card achieves high participation.
The deadlines were demanding: the CPSC would have had to propose a rule within 90 days and finalize it within 270 days, a schedule that could strain the agency and invite a rushed or litigated rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is favorable but modest. The mechanism is cheap — a simplified postcard or a web form — and borrows a model (child car seat registration) with a documented track record of raising recall compliance, aimed at products where defects kill or injure small children. The costs are real but small: printing, data handling, and some privacy risk contained by the recall-only restriction. This was not a sweeping overhaul of product safety law; it addressed one narrow failure point — that almost nobody hears about a recall — with a low-cost fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Moran introduced the bill on March 1, 2005, joined by Rep. Jim McGovern as its only cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three weeks later, on March 22, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed; the bill died in subcommittee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of juvenile products and small appliances were better off, because they avoided new registration and notification requirements. Families that buy cribs, strollers, and appliances gained nothing: they remain reliant on news reports and store postings to learn about recalls.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Product makers avoided new costs; parents gained nothing

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its consumer protection subcommittee on March 22, 2005 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no one's position was recorded; both sponsors were Democrats and the bill died without action in the Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee.

industries.industry: Juvenile product manufacturers (cribs, strollers, high chairs, toys)
industries.note: The bill's core covered category. These makers would have to include a registration card or run online registration with every unit and maintain recall-only contact databases. Their interest in the status quo — relying on news coverage and the 7%-of-buyers registration rate — runs directly against parents' interest in hearing about a recall before a child is hurt.

Toaster, blender, coffee maker, and food processor makers were the bill's other explicitly covered category, facing the same registration and database obligations. The costs are modest per unit but fall on a low-margin industry.

The bill encouraged but did not require retailers to help with recall notification, and CPSC staff currently lean on retailers and the media to spread recall news. Retailers would face little direct mandate but could share more of the notification burden in practice.
